clinicalPearls: MEN1 is characterized primarily by the triad of parathyroid, pancreatic islet, and pituitary tumors (the '3 Ps'); it is an autosomal dominant syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392/ch.388).
MEN2 predisposes to medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3079).

There are three familial forms of MTC: MEN 2A, MEN 2B, and familial MTC without other features of MEN; MTC is more aggressive in MEN 2B than in MEN 2A, and familial MTC is more aggressive than sporadic MTC (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).

MEN1 is caused by inactivating germline mutations of the MEN1 (menin) tumor-suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13; about half of affected patients develop prolactinomas, while acromegaly and Cushing's disease are less common (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392).

MEN2 is caused by activating point mutations of the RET protooncogene (a receptor tyrosine kinase) in a single allele, in contrast to the tumor-suppressor loss-of-function mechanism of MEN1 (Harrison 22e p.3079).

Early genetic screening for RET mutations identifies individuals at risk for MEN2 who may benefit from prophylactic thyroidectomy and biochemical screening for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3079).

All patients with MTC should be tested for RET mutations, because genetic counseling and cascade testing of family members can then be offered to those who test positive (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).
harrison.pathophysiology: MEN1 follows the two-hit tumor-suppressor paradigm: the affected individual inherits a mutant copy of the MEN1 gene (menin, chromosome 11q13), and tumorigenesis follows a somatic 'second hit' (deletion or point mutation) that inactivates the remaining normal allele. In contrast, MEN2 is caused by activating point mutations in a single allele of the RET protooncogene, encoding a receptor tyrosine kinase; constitutive RET activity leads to thyroid C-cell hyperplasia in childhood that precedes the development of medullary thyroid carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.388/ch.397).
nonInfectiousMimics: Other familial pituitary tumor / endocrine neoplasia syndromes: MEN 4 (CDKN1B mutation; hyperparathyroidism and pituitary adenomas), Carney complex (PRKAR1A; spotty skin pigmentation, myxomas, endocrine tumors), McCune-Albright syndrome, and familial isolated pituitary adenomas (AIP) (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392).
Other inherited predispositions to pheochromocytoma that overlap with MEN2: von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis, and hereditary paraganglioma syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.247).
additionalInvestigations: Germline RET mutation testing in all patients with medullary thyroid carcinoma, with cascade screening of relatives (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).
MEN1 (menin) gene testing in patients with the parathyroid/pancreatic-islet/pituitary tumor pattern or relevant family history (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392/ch.376).
Biochemical screening for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism in RET-mutation carriers identified as at risk for MEN2 (Harrison 22e p.3079).
redFlags: Exclude pheochromocytoma BEFORE any surgery: prior to surgery, pheochromocytoma should be excluded in all patients with a RET mutation (failure to do so risks an intraoperative hypertensive crisis) (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).
MTC in the context of MEN 2B carries a more aggressive course than MEN 2A and warrants early/prophylactic intervention (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis is driven by the component tumors and genotype. MTC is more aggressive in MEN 2B than in MEN 2A, and familial MTC is more aggressive than sporadic MTC; early genetic identification permits prophylactic thyroidectomy before malignant transformation, improving outcome (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).
pitfalls: Proceeding to surgery (e.g., thyroidectomy or parathyroid surgery) without first excluding an unsuspected pheochromocytoma in a RET-mutation carrier (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).
Failing to perform RET testing in all MTC patients and thereby missing cascade screening opportunities for at-risk family members (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).
management: Genotype-directed prophylactic total thyroidectomy in RET-mutation carriers, with total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection for established medullary thyroid carcinoma and tyrosine-kinase inhibitors such as vandetanib or cabozantinib for advanced disease
Exclude and treat phaeochromocytoma before any surgery, using alpha- then beta-adrenergic blockade followed by adrenalectomy

In MEN1, parathyroidectomy for hyperparathyroidism, proton-pump inhibitors for gastrinoma-driven Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and surgical or medical treatment of pancreatic neuroendocrine and pituitary tumours including dopamine agonists for prolactinoma
Germline RET or MEN1 mutation testing of the index case with cascade genetic screening of at-risk relatives
Lifelong biochemical and imaging surveillance for the syndrome's component tumours
Genetic counselling for these autosomal dominant conditions
Coordinated multidisciplinary endocrine, surgical and oncological care
